lessons.title: Electrolysis
lessons.summary: Understand how electricity splits ionic compounds apart, predict the products of electrolysing molten salts and aqueous solutions, and see how aluminium is extracted on an industrial scale.
objectives: I can explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved.
I can predict the products at each electrode when a molten ionic compound is electrolysed.
I can use the rules for aqueous solutions to predict which gas or metal forms at each electrode.
I can describe the extraction of aluminium from aluminium oxide, including the role of cryolite and why the anodes are replaced.
I can write half equations for reactions at the electrodes (Higher).

activities.title: What electrolysis is
activities.content:
## Splitting compounds with electricity

**Electrolysis** means using an electric current to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The word literally means "splitting with electricity".

The set-up has three parts:

- The **electrolyte**: the ionic compound, either **molten** or **dissolved in water**.
- Two **electrodes**, usually made of inert (unreactive) graphite or platinum, dipped into the electrolyte.
- A **DC power supply** connected to the electrodes.

The electrode connected to the positive terminal is the **anode** (+). The electrode connected to the negative terminal is the **cathode** (−).

### Why molten or dissolved?

A solid ionic compound cannot be electrolysed. Its ions are locked in a giant lattice and cannot move. When the compound melts or dissolves, the ions become **free to move**, so they can carry the current and travel to the electrodes.

### Which ion goes where?

Opposites attract:

- **Positive ions (cations)**, usually metal ions or H⁺, move to the **negative cathode**.
- **Negative ions (anions)**, such as Cl⁻, Br⁻ or O²⁻, move to the **positive anode**.

A memory aid: **PANIC** — Positive is Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

activities.title: Worked example: molten lead bromide
activities.content:
**Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. What forms at each electrode?**

First identify the ions: **Pb²⁺** and **Br⁻**.

**At the cathode (−):** Pb²⁺ ions are attracted. Each ion gains two electrons and becomes a lead atom. Molten silver-grey lead collects at the bottom.

Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb

Gaining electrons is **reduction**, so the cathode is where reduction happens.

**At the anode (+):** Br⁻ ions are attracted. Each loses one electron. Two bromine atoms then join to make a Br₂ molecule, seen as brown fumes.

2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

Losing electrons is **oxidation**, so oxidation always happens at the anode.

**Overall:** PbBr₂ → Pb + Br₂

The pattern for any **molten** binary compound is simple: **metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode**.

question.hint: Metal ions are positive and go to the negative electrode.

activities.title: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
activities.content:
## Water gets involved

When the electrolyte is a solution in water, there are extra ions to consider. Water itself splits very slightly into **H⁺** and **OH⁻** ions. So at each electrode there is a competition.

### At the cathode (−): metal ion or H⁺?

The **less reactive** one is discharged.

- If the metal is **more reactive than hydrogen** (sodium, potassium, magnesium, zinc and so on), **hydrogen gas** forms instead of the metal.
- If the metal is **less reactive than hydrogen** (copper, silver, gold), the **metal** is deposited.

### At the anode (+): halide ion or OH⁻?

- If the solution contains a **halide ion** (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻), the **halogen** forms (chlorine, bromine, iodine).
- Otherwise (sulfates, nitrates, and so on) **oxygen** forms from the hydroxide ions.

### Summary table

| Solution | Cathode | Anode |
|---|---|---|
| copper(II) chloride | copper | chlorine |
| copper(II) sulfate | copper | oxygen |
| sodium chloride | hydrogen | chlorine |
| sodium sulfate | hydrogen | oxygen |

When hydrogen is produced at the cathode, the OH⁻ ions are left behind, so the solution becomes **alkaline**. Electrolysis of brine (sodium chloride solution) is how sodium hydroxide is made industrially.

activities.title: Worked example: potassium bromide solution
activities.content:
**Predict the products when aqueous potassium bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes.**

**Ions present:** K⁺ and Br⁻ from the salt, plus H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.

**Cathode:** K⁺ or H⁺? Potassium is far more reactive than hydrogen, so **hydrogen gas** is produced. You would see bubbles of a colourless gas.

2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

**Anode:** Br⁻ or OH⁻? Bromide is a halide, so **bromine** is produced. The solution near the anode turns orange-brown.

2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

**Left in solution:** K⁺ and OH⁻, which is potassium hydroxide. Universal indicator would turn purple near the cathode.

**Contrast this with silver nitrate solution:** silver is less reactive than hydrogen, so **silver** coats the cathode, and because nitrate is not a halide, **oxygen** forms at the anode.

question.text: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using inert graphite electrodes. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen. Sulfate is not a halide.
question.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so copper metal is deposited on the cathode. Sulfate is not a halide, so oxygen (from OH⁻ ions) is produced at the anode. The blue colour fades as Cu²⁺ ions are removed.

options.text: Copper is deposited on the cathode.
Oxygen gas is produced at the anode.
Hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode.
options.feedback: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper is discharged instead.

options.text: Sulfur is produced at the anode.
options.feedback: Sulfate ions are not discharged; hydroxide ions give oxygen instead.

activities.title: Half equations (Higher)
activities.content:
## Writing what happens at each electrode

A **half equation** shows the electrons being gained or lost at one electrode.

**Cathode (reduction, electrons gained):** electrons appear on the **left**.

- Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
- Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
- 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

**Anode (oxidation, electrons lost):** electrons appear on the **right**.

- 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
- 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
- 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
- 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻

### Checking a half equation

1. **Atoms must balance.** Two chloride ions are needed to make one Cl₂ molecule.
2. **Charge must balance.** On the left of 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ the charge is 2−; on the right it is 0 + (2−) = 2−. Balanced.

The oxygen equation from hydroxide is the one students find hardest. Four OH⁻ ions give one O₂ molecule, two water molecules and four electrons. Count the atoms: 4 O and 4 H on both sides. Count the charge: 4− on both sides.

activities.title: Extracting aluminium
activities.content:
## Aluminium: too reactive for carbon

Aluminium is **above carbon** in the reactivity series, so its oxide cannot be reduced by heating with carbon. Instead, aluminium oxide (from the ore **bauxite**) is electrolysed.

### The problem of melting point

Pure aluminium oxide melts at over 2000 °C, which would cost a fortune in energy. The solution is to dissolve the aluminium oxide in **molten cryolite**. This mixture melts at a much lower temperature (around 950 °C), so it saves energy and money. Cryolite also improves the conductivity of the electrolyte.

### What happens at the electrodes

Both electrodes are made of **graphite (carbon)**.

**Cathode (−):** aluminium ions gain electrons and molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.

Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al

**Anode (+):** oxide ions lose electrons and oxygen gas forms.

2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻

### Why the anodes burn away

The oxygen produced at the hot graphite anodes reacts with the carbon to form **carbon dioxide**. The anodes gradually get smaller and must be **replaced regularly**. This is an ongoing cost of the process.

### Why aluminium is expensive

Electrolysis needs a very large electric current running continuously, plus energy to keep the electrolyte molten, plus replacement anodes. That is why recycling aluminium, which needs only about 5% of the energy, is so worthwhile.

activities.title: Worked example: reading an exam question about aluminium
activities.content:
**"Explain why cryolite is used, and why the positive electrodes need replacing." (4 marks)**

A full-mark answer hits four separate points:

1. Aluminium oxide has a **very high melting point**.
2. Dissolving it in molten cryolite **lowers the melting point** (or lowers the temperature needed), which **reduces the energy cost**.
3. **Oxygen** is produced at the positive electrodes (anodes).
4. The oxygen **reacts with the carbon** of the electrodes to form **carbon dioxide**, so the anodes wear away.

Notice the structure: each point is a cause or an effect, in a chain. Examiners reward clear cause-and-effect chains, so use words like "so" and "because".

**A common lost mark:** writing "cryolite makes it melt" without explaining that this saves energy. Always finish the chain.

question.text: Put these stages of aluminium extraction into the correct order.
question.hint: The oxide must be dissolved before any current can pass.
question.explanation: Bauxite is purified to aluminium oxide, dissolved in molten cryolite, then electrolysed; aluminium forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, where it burns the carbon away.
order: Aluminium oxide is obtained from bauxite ore
The oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point
A current is passed through the molten mixture
Aluminium collects at the cathode and oxygen forms at the anode
Oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes, which must be replaced

question.text:
A student electrolyses sodium chloride solution using inert electrodes.

(a) Name the gas formed at the negative electrode, and explain why sodium metal is not formed.

(b) Name the gas formed at the positive electrode and describe a test for it.

(c) The student adds universal indicator to the solution after electrolysis. State what colour it turns and explain why.
question.hint: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen. Chloride is a halide. Think about which ions are left in the solution.
question.explanation: (a) Hydrogen, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so H⁺ ions from water are discharged instead of Na⁺. (b) Chlorine, which bleaches damp blue litmus paper (turning it white). (c) Blue or purple, because Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain, forming sodium hydroxide, an alkali.

markScheme.criterion: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged instead
Test: damp (blue) litmus paper is bleached / turns white
Indicator turns blue/purple because hydroxide ions (sodium hydroxide) are left, making the solution alkaline

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Electrolysis uses a **DC current** to split an ionic compound that is **molten or dissolved** so its ions can move.
- **Cathode (−)**: positive ions gain electrons (**reduction**). **Anode (+)**: negative ions lose electrons (**oxidation**).
- **Molten compound**: metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode.
- **Aqueous solution**: hydrogen at the cathode if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; halogen at the anode if a halide is present, otherwise oxygen.
- **Aluminium**: Al₂O₃ dissolved in **molten cryolite** (lowers melting point, saves energy); Al at the cathode, O₂ at the anode; carbon anodes burn to CO₂ and must be replaced.
- Half equations: electrons on the **left** for reduction, on the **right** for oxidation; atoms and charge must balance.

practiceQuestions.text:
Aluminium is extracted by the electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite.

(a) Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by heating its oxide with carbon.

(b) Explain why the process is expensive.

(c) Suggest why recycling aluminium is better for the environment than extracting it from bauxite.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the reactivity series, the energy used by the electrolysis cell, and what recycling avoids.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide. (b) Large amounts of electricity are needed to run the cell and keep the electrolyte molten, and the carbon anodes have to be replaced regularly. (c) Recycling uses far less energy (around 5%), so it produces less carbon dioxide, and it avoids quarrying bauxite and the waste it produces.

markScheme.criterion: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon (above carbon in the reactivity series)
Large amount of electrical energy needed (to pass the current and/or keep the electrolyte molten)
Carbon anodes burn away and must be replaced regularly
Recycling uses much less energy / produces less carbon dioxide / avoids mining bauxite

practiceQuestions.text: A lump of solid copper(II) sulfate does not conduct electricity, but a solution of copper(II) sulfate in water does. Why?
practiceQuestions.hint: Electrolysis needs charged particles that can travel to the electrodes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In the solid, the Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions are locked in a lattice. When the compound dissolves the ions separate and are free to move, so they can carry the current.

options.text: In the solid the ions are fixed in place; in solution the ions are free to move.
The solid contains no ions until water is added.
options.feedback: The ions are already there in the solid, but they cannot move.

options.text: The water supplies free electrons that carry the current.
options.feedback: Water does not provide free electrons; moving ions carry the charge in an electrolyte.

options.text: Dissolving changes the ions into neutral atoms.
options.feedback: Dissolving separates the ions; it does not remove their charges.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Pb²⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode, where they gain electrons and form lead. Br⁻ ions are attracted to the anode, where they lose electrons (oxidation) to form bromine.

Chlorine gas is produced at the anode.
Hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode.
